Where do we use this in real life? You and your brother both have ten sweets, and you give him three. Now you have seven and he has thirteen, so he is six ahead, not three! Moving three changes the gap by six. One side loses three, and the other gains three.

Where do we use this in real life? The Lions lead the Tigers three to two, but the referee says one Lions goal really belongs to the Tigers. Now it is two to three: only one goal moved, but the gap changed by two. Moving one changes the gap by two. One side loses one, and the other gains one.

Where do we use this in real life? Shelf A has twenty books and Shelf B has twelve, a gap of eight. Move just half the gap, four books, and both shelves have sixteen. To make two groups equal, move half the gap.

Where do we use this in real life? The red and blue piggy banks both have twelve coins. Move five coins from red to blue and it is seven and seventeen, so blue has ten more: five lost plus five gained. Moving five changes the gap by ten. One side loses five, and the other gains five.

Where do we use this in real life? On the MRT, Carriage one has forty passengers and Carriage two has thirty, a gap of ten. Only half the gap, five people, need to walk to the next carriage, and then both have thirty-five. To make two groups equal, move half the gap.

Where do we use this in real life? For the class party, ice cream has sixteen votes and bubble tea has fourteen. When two children switch to bubble tea it is fourteen to sixteen, because each switch changes the gap by two. Moving two changes the gap by four. One side loses two, and the other gains two.

Where do we use this in real life? The red and blue tug-of-war teams both have six players. If one player switches to blue, it is five against seven, so blue has two more, not one! Moving one changes the gap by two. One side loses one, and the other gains one.

Where do we use this in real life? Table A has nine chairs and Table B has five. Move three chairs over and it is six and eight, so the gap changed by six, twice the three you moved. Moving three changes the gap by six. One side loses three, and the other gains three.
